title: How to add a formula in Numbers on Mac: step by step for Numbers 15.4
metaTitle: How to Add a Formula in Numbers on Mac (Step by Step)
description: Learn how to add a formula in Numbers on Mac: click a cell, type =, add cells and operators, then press Return. Steps for Numbers 15.4.
targetKeyword: how to add a formula in numbers on mac
intro: Click the empty cell where you want the result, then type an equal sign (=). Add cell references, numbers and operators such as +, -, * and /, then press Return or click Commit Formula to save it.
tldr: Click an empty cell, type = to start the formula, then click cells or type values and operators.
Press Return or Tab, or click Commit Formula, to save. Press Esc to throw the change away.
Select a range and use the Insert button in the toolbar to drop in a formula for the whole range.
A blank cell can mean Numbers is hiding an error. Click the error to read the message.
Numbers 15.4 requires macOS 26 or later. Check your version in the App Store first.

blocks.text: Formulas in Numbers work the way they do in most spreadsheet apps. You start with an equal sign, point at the cells you want to use, and then save. This guide covers Numbers 15.4 on a Mac. Menu labels and shortcuts can shift a little between versions, so each step describes what you should see on screen.
What you need before you start

Numbers 15.4 for Mac requires macOS 26 or later, according to Apple's What's new page. TidBITS reports that the 15.4 release is out. Some functions in 15.4, such as XOR and COMBINA, need that version. A reader comment on TidBITS says a UK Apple page still showed 15.3, so check the version in the App Store before you hunt for a menu item that isn't there.

items: A Mac running macOS 26 or later
Numbers 15.4 or later, installed from the App Store
A table on the sheet you're working on
The cells that will feed the formula already filled in

blocks.text: Type a formula directly into a cell

This is the method most people use, and it's the one to learn first. Click the empty cell where the answer belongs. Type an equal sign (=). Numbers opens the Formula Editor, and the Functions Browser appears with it. Then type your formula, or click cells to add them.

The Formula Editor moves and resizes. Drag its left side to move it out of the way of your table. Drag an outer edge to make it bigger or smaller. This helps when a formula runs long and you need to see the cells behind it.

blocks.title: Why the equal sign matters
blocks.text: Without the equal sign, Numbers doesn't open the Formula Editor. You're just typing into the cell. Start with = every time you want a calculation.
Build a formula from cells, values and operators

Here's a simple case. Say you want the total of a column. Click the result cell, type =, then click the first cell in the column. Type +, then click the next cell. Keep going until every cell you need is in the formula, then save it.

You can also type a plain value when a number isn't in the table. The operators are +, -, * and /. Use parentheses to control the order of the math, such as (A + B) * C, when the order changes the answer.
Clicking cells gets slow on a long column. That's when a function helps. Functions handle common jobs so you don't have to click every cell. Use the Functions Browser to find the one you need.
Use the Functions Browser to find a function

The Functions Browser opens when you type =. Use its search field to find a function by name. Double-click a function, and Numbers adds it to the Formula Editor. Then fill in its arguments with cell references or values.

If you don't know the function's name, try a short search and read the results. Then check the reference in Help before you commit the formula. Wrong arguments are the most common reason a function fails to give you what you expected.
Add a formula to a range with the Insert button

The toolbar Insert button is a faster route when the formula covers a whole range. Select the cells you want to use first. Click Insert in the toolbar and choose a formula. Numbers inserts the formula and picks a cell for the result.

Apple's guide describes this in general terms. Some other guides write the menu item as New Formula or Formula. Read the label in your own copy of Numbers, because wording can change between versions. If you don't see the option, check that the range is selected.
Keyboard shortcuts for formulas on Mac

Apple's Numbers keyboard page writes the modifier keys in words, such as Command and Option. The table below uses the symbols you see in menus. ⌘ is Command, ⌥ is Option, ⌃ is Control and ⇧ is Shift. Some shortcuts can be changed in System Settings, so your keys may differ.

blocks.caption: Shortcuts from Apple's Numbers keyboard page. Check them in your version.

blocks.text: Two of these need care. According to Apple's list, ⌃= also converts an open formula to text. Press it only when you mean to lose the formula. ⌘Return stops cell editing, but it doesn't save a formula, so it's the wrong key for committing.

blocks.title: Don't use ⌘Return to save
blocks.text: Apple lists ⌘Return for stopping cell editing. Use Return, Tab or the Commit Formula button to save the formula into the cell.
A survey of marketing and sales staff found that many struggle with formulas. Other coverage of that survey gives a different figure, so treat the number as a rough signal.
Look up what a function does before you use it

Apple's Formulas and Functions help covers more than 300 functions. Open Help in the menu bar and choose Formulas and Functions Help. The reference explains the types of arguments, conditions and wildcards each function supports.

Numbers 15.4 added more. Apple's What's new page lists trigonometry, statistics and logic functions, including XOR, COMBINA, DAYS and PEARSON. If a formula fails on an older version, check whether it needs a newer release of Numbers.
If you want the reference in a browser, Apple also links to an online guide at support.apple.com/guide/functions/.
Read and fix a formula error

Numbers hides a formula's result until the error is fixed. The cell can look empty even after you commit the formula. Click the error to read its message. Apple's example is a function with a blank argument, which stays an error until you give it a value.

VoiceOver users can press VO Space to open the Formula Editor and fix the error. Apple says VoiceOver reads the error message as part of the cell description, so you hear the problem without hunting for it.

blocks.text: Mistakes people make when adding formulas

items: Skipping the equal sign, so Numbers never opens the Formula Editor
Pressing ⌘Return and expecting the formula to save
Pressing Esc and then wondering where the formula went, since Esc discards changes
Leaving a function argument blank and missing the error that follows
Using the Insert button without selecting the range first

blocks.text: Formulas on iCloud and suggested formulas costs

The web version of Numbers on iCloud.com has its own list of differences. Apple's list covers pivot-table limits, view-only equations, 3D charts and Apple Intelligence. It doesn't name spreadsheet formulas. No formula-by-formula comparison turned up, so test your formula on iCloud before you rely on it.

Numbers also has a pattern-based suggestion feature. It can suggest data or generate formulas from patterns in your table. MacRumors reports that Apple lists it under Numbers features for Creator Studio subscribers, not for all users. Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year, with a one-month free trial for new subscribers.
Numbers itself stays free to use, according to Apple's Creator Studio page. Typing formulas by hand, as this guide shows, doesn't need a subscription.
Where to go next

Once the formula works, you might want to reorder the rows. Our guide on [sorting a table in Numbers on Mac by column](/how-to/sort-a-table-by-column-in-numbers) walks through that. If you reuse the sheet each week, save a copy with the formulas intact before you change the data.

faq.question: Can I add a formula in Numbers on Mac without typing it?
faq.answer: Partly. Select a range of cells, click Insert in the toolbar, and choose a formula. Numbers inserts it and picks a result cell. A pattern-based suggestion feature can also generate formulas, but Apple lists it for Creator Studio subscribers.

faq.question: Do I have to pay to add formulas in Numbers?
faq.answer: No. Numbers stays free to use, and typing formulas by hand doesn't need a subscription. Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year, with a one-month free trial for new subscribers.

faq.question: Why does my formula cell look empty?
faq.answer: Numbers hides the result while the formula has an error. Click the error to read the message. A blank function argument is one common cause, and Apple uses it as its example.

faq.question: Which Numbers version do I need for the newest functions?
faq.answer: Numbers 15.4 adds functions such as XOR and COMBINA, and it requires macOS 26 or later. Check the version in the App Store, because a TidBITS reader reported that a UK Apple page still showed 15.3.

faq.question: Is a formula the same in Numbers on iCloud?
faq.answer: Apple's iCloud differences page doesn't name spreadsheet formulas. It does list pivot-table limits and view-only equations. Test a formula in the browser version before you rely on it.

faq.question: Where can I see every function Numbers supports?
faq.answer: Open Help in the menu bar and choose Formulas and Functions Help. Apple says the help covers more than 300 functions. Apple also links to an online guide at support.apple.com/guide/functions/.

task: Add a formula to a cell in Numbers on Mac
appliesTo: Numbers 15.4 on Mac, macOS 26 or later
requirements: A Mac running macOS 26 or later
A table on the sheet you're working on
Cells that will feed the formula already filled in

steps.name: Click the cell for your result
steps.text: Click the empty cell where the answer should appear. Formulas go in table cells, so make sure the cell sits in a table on your sheet. The result shows up in this cell once the formula is saved.

steps.name: Type an equal sign
steps.text: Type = (equal sign). The Formula Editor opens, and the Functions Browser appears with it. If the cell already holds content you want to edit in the editor, press ⌃= instead.
steps.tip: Typing a number or a word first doesn't open the editor. Delete what you typed, then press =.

steps.name: Add cells, values and operators
steps.text: Click a cell to add its reference, or type a plain value. Type an operator between parts, such as +, -, * or /. Keep going until the formula says what you need.

steps.name: Add a function if you need one
steps.text: Type a function name in the search field of the Functions Browser. Double-click the function you want, and it moves into the Formula Editor. Fill in its arguments with cells or values.

steps.name: Read the formula, then save it
steps.text: Read the whole formula in the editor. Check that each cell reference points at the cell you meant. Then press Return or Tab, or click the Commit Formula button to save.
steps.tip: Command Return doesn't save a formula. Apple lists it for stopping cell editing.

steps.name: Close without saving if you change your mind
steps.text: Press Esc to discard your changes in the Formula Editor. You can also click the Close button, which exits without saving.
steps.tip: Closing and committing are different. Only committing keeps the formula in the cell.

steps.name: Insert a formula over a selected range
steps.text: Select the range of cells you want the formula to work on. Click the Insert button in the toolbar and choose a formula. Numbers inserts the formula and picks a result cell. Apple's guide describes this in general terms, and labels vary by version, so read the label on your screen.

steps.name: Edit a formula you already added
steps.text: Double-click the cell that holds the formula, or select it and press ⌥Return. The Formula Editor opens with the formula ready to change. Make your edits, then press Return or Tab to save.

steps.name: Open the function reference
steps.text: Click Help in the menu bar and choose Formulas and Functions Help. The reference covers more than 300 functions and the argument types each one accepts. Use it when a function's arguments aren't clear.

shortcuts.action: Open the editor with the cell's current contents

troubleshooting.problem: The cell is blank after I saved the formula
troubleshooting.fix: Numbers hides the result while the formula has an error. Click the error to read the message, then fix the cause. A blank function argument is a common reason.
Check that you're still in the Formula Editor. Press Return or Tab again, or click Commit Formula. Command Return doesn't save a formula.
Click the cell once so it's selected, then type = again. If the cell already has content, press ⌃= to open the editor with what's in it.

troubleshooting.problem: I can't find the formula option under Insert
troubleshooting.fix: Select the range first. Then look for the formula option under the Insert button in the toolbar. Labels vary by version, so the exact wording may differ.
You probably pressed Esc, which discards changes, or clicked Close, which exits without saving. Type the formula again and save it with Return or Tab.

troubleshooting.problem: I want the formula written for me
troubleshooting.fix: Pattern-based formula suggestions are listed for Apple Creator Studio subscribers, not all users. Creator Studio costs $12.99 per month or $129 per year, with a one-month free trial for new subscribers. Typing the formula by hand, as in this guide, needs no subscription.
